edge_1003.relationship: LaRocque: cross-cultural ethnological description of Native and Métis women as othering, 1999
edge_1003.evidence_note: This arrow represents Emma LaRocque's specified criticism in her 1999 University of Manitoba dissertation (read at PDF pp. 54 and 249), not a verdict of the Indigenous history entry. She describes 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s-1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)', which 'tended to frame all things Native in typical terms of "cultural differences" or "traditions."' She grants: 'Compared to earlier racist material, this is, of course, a much improved approach to Native history. And with greater awareness, there is greater improvement.' But 'ethnological descriptions have a "distancing" effect', and 'This process results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable to his or her audience' (p. 249). Her note 18 names the book: 'See in Many Tender Ties, for example, Van Kirk's listing of all the items of fashion or jewelry metis women were "very fond of" (101-103). There is an unstated assumption that such interests are abnormal or "remarkable" for these women to acquire' (p. 249, n. 18). In an earlier note she cites the book, with Saum and Ray and Freeman, among fur-trade studies that record Native resistance (PDF p. 54, note). Brown is named in the same list on p. 249 and the criticism is noted on her own entry (pe139_brown_rel_01); one arrow is drawn, to Van Kirk, because the note's example is hers. edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer) already carries LaRocque with Sioui and Stevenson (Wheeler) at entry level; this edge records the person-level target. OCR slips in the PDF text layer are corrected ('Van Krk', 'al1', 'hrterests'). The page numbers are PDF pages, as in edge_868. No identity classification is recorded. Later reading, labelled: Perry (2008, p. 163) dates 'sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques' of Van Kirk's work to the early 1990s; those texts are unread here.

indigenous.label: Indigenous-authored history & critique
indigenous.date_label: Earlier witnesses 1615–1938 · critiques of the academy 1969–99 · refusal, resurgence and peoplehood 2007–17
indigenous.description: Historical writing, criticism and theory by Indigenous authors, from early manuscript and print witnesses to academic history and political theory. It is plural: Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Dakota, Māori, Hawaiian and Aboriginal traditions have their own roots and are not branches of one academic field. From 1969 Deloria, Adams, LaRocque, Sioui, Trask and Smith turned criticism on the institutions and disciplines that studied them; LaRocque judged that 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (1999). After 2000 the criticism became theory: Audra Simpson's 'ethnographic refusal' (2007, 2014); Coulthard's case against 'the politics of recognition' (2009, 2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's resurgence, which turns from efforts to 'Indigenize the academy' toward 'a resurgence of Indigenous intellectual systems' (2014); Andersen's Métis 'peoplehood' against 'mixedness' (2014). Older university scholarship about Indigenous peoples and community-engaged research have their own entries; settler colonial studies is a comparative field.
indigenous.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier witnesses: Guaman Poma (c. 1615/1616), Cusick (checked 1828 edition), Apess (1836), Te Rangikāheke (manuscripts before 1854), Warren (1885), Thunderchild and Ahenakew (1923; 1929), Pei Te Hurinui Jones (1929), Mathews (1932, 1961), Te Rangi Hīroa (1938, 1949), McNickle (1949; Native American Tribalism, 1973). Critiques 1969–99: Deloria, Custer Died for Your Sins (1969); Adams, Prison of Grass (1975); LaRocque, Defeathering the Indian (1975) and her dissertation (1999); Dickason (1984, 1992); Sioui (1989); Walker (1990); Trask, 'Natives and Anthropologists' (1991) and From a Native Daughter (1993); Kameʻeleihiwa (1992); Wilson (1996); O'Brien (1997); Rigney (1999); Smith, Decolonizing Methodologies (1999). After 2000: Audra Simpson, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007) and Mohawk Interruptus (2014); Coulthard, Red Skin, White Masks (2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), 'Land as pedagogy' (2014), As We Have Always Done (2017); Andersen, 'Métis' (2014); Moreton-Robinson, The White Possessive (2015). See the strands for works, collaborators and evidence limits.

indigenous.scope_note: Part 2 of the Indigenous histories family (split in revision 1.201): history, criticism and theory by Indigenous authors. Membership rests on Indigenous authorship or co-authorship sourced person by person, in the author's own words or an institutional or publisher profile (see the people records), never inferred from a name or a topic. Collaborative and community-directed research has its own entry; settler scholarship about Indigenous peoples is in Ethnohistory and Indigenous–newcomer relations; settler colonial studies is a comparative field. Reviewed through 2017. Read in full: Audra Simpson 2007; Trask 1991 with Keesing's reply; Nicoll's 2015 review of Simpson and Moreton-Robinson. strands.focus: Apess challenges colonial historical judgments and Pilgrim celebration. His Christian moral argument is an earlier intervention; no borrowing by later theorists is asserted.

strands.focus: Te Rangikāheke’s genealogy and historical narration survive within manuscripts and Grey’s altered publications. Attribution reveals an Indigenous author behind texts circulated under a governor’s name.
strands.works: Historical and genealogical manuscripts before 1854; material reused in Grey’s publications, 1853–55

strands.title: Cree narration and interwar writing
strands.focus: Thunderchild’s narration, Ahenakew’s 1923 recording and literary writing, his 1929 publication, and the 1973 edited book carry different dates and authorial roles. Cuthand’s 1995 criticism makes editorial selection visible.
strands.works: 1923 narration/recording; Cree Trickster Tales (1929); Voices of the Plains Cree (1973; 1995 introduction)

strands.title: Tainui genealogies and historical writing
strands.focus: Jones’s Māori-language historical work and the history of its publication distinguish interwar research from the 1995 posthumous volume. The institutional biography describes disputed reuse of an earlier English manuscript.
strands.works: Māhinārangi (1929); English historical manuscript by c. 1936; Ngā iwi o Tainui (1995, posthumous)

strands.title: Canadian historical synthesis and regional inquiry
strands.focus: Dickason’s studies of representations and historical synthesis sit alongside Stonechild and Waiser’s Saskatchewan study. These are different scales and collaborations, not one doctrinal programme.
strands.works: The Myth of the Savage (1984); Canada’s First Nations (1992); Stonechild and Waiser, Loyal Till Death (1997)

strands.title: Métis scholarship and criticism of representation
strands.focus: Adams’s colonial and class interpretation and LaRocque’s criticism of representation broaden the 1970s bibliography. Her 1999 dissertation p. 34 explicitly connects the earlier book to curriculum research and resistance. These are distinct intellectual positions. The dissertation names its targets: James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing ('Canadian historiography is not that benign'), Trigger's foreword to Sioui as 'a language of containment', and the 'neo cross-cultural approach' of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk; Adams is her 'Metis historian and social critic' (PDF pp. 47, 119, 135–136, 249). When the Other Is Me (2011) is the revised book.
strands.works: Prison of Grass (1975); Defeathering the Indian (1975)

strands.title: Wendat autohistory and historical interpretation
strands.focus: Sioui’s author interview supplies an explicit historiographical proposal about self-interpretation and oral transmission. His moral account remains attributed and situated; French and English publication dates are distinct.
strands.works: Pour une autohistoire amérindienne (1989); author interview (1991); English translation by Sheila Fischman (1992)

strands.title: Historical synthesis and Native history institutions
strands.focus: McNickle’s 1949 work and role in creating the Newberry centre in 1972 establish an earlier bibliography and institutional contribution. Neither the centre nor a university is treated as the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge. His 1973 preface challenged administrators' 'certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress'; Iverson (1993) noted that 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience'. He helped found the NCAI (1944), organised the Workshops on American Indian Affairs from 1960, and directed the Newberry centre in its first fellowship year (1973–74).
strands.works: They Came Here First: The Epic of the American Indian (1949); Newberry history centre (1972)

strands.title: Osage historical writing across the century
strands.focus: Mathews’s 1932 work and 1961 history supply earlier and mid-century examples. The publisher describes oral and documentary historical resources; detailed methodological claims await the works.
strands.works: Wah’Kon-Tah (1932); The Osages: Children of the Middle Waters (1961)

strands.title: Hawaiian land history and sovereignty
strands.focus: Kameʻeleihiwa’s land history and Trask’s political essays provide distinct Hawaiian contributions. Hawaiian-language historiography has earlier authors; neither regional programme is a subset of the Māori examples. In 1991 Trask answered Keesing's charge that Pacific nationalists 'invent' their pasts: genealogy is 'solid evidence from Native forms of history', and Hawaiians do not want 'to be "liberated" from our past'. Keesing replied that her 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy was 'a great leap backward'; Linnekin, that 'Traditions are neither genuine nor spurious'.
strands.works: Native Land and Foreign Desires (1992); From a Native Daughter (1993; revised 1999)

strands.title: Aboriginal interviews and life writing
strands.focus: Gilbert’s interviews and Ginibi’s autobiography broaden the historical bibliography beyond university monographs. Their forms and authorial positions differ from each other and from community-transmitted oral histories.
strands.works: Living Black (1977); Don’t Take Your Love to Town (1988)

strands.title: Refusal, resurgence and the critique of recognition
strands.focus: Three linked but distinct arguments, each with its own target. Audra Simpson proposed 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' in Iroquois studies and made refusal a method: ethnography as a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in' (2007); Mohawk Interruptus (2014) carries the argument into Kahnawà:ke's history and Morgan and Parker's ethnology. Coulthard challenged 'the now commonplace assumption' that colonial relations in Canada 'can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition', using Fanon against Taylor and reworking Marx: 'dispossession, not proletarianization' shaped Indigenous–state relations (2009; book 2014). Leanne Betasamosake Simpson defined resurgence as 'the rebuilding of Indigenous nations according to our own political, intellectual and cultural traditions' and met the academy's 'colonial refusal' with 'Indigenous refusal' (2014), citing Coulthard on recognition and Simpson on refusal. Alfred's Wasáse (2005) is a shared reference. In the pages read none of them criticises Wolfe.
strands.works: Audra Simpson, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007), Mohawk Interruptus (2014); Glen Sean Coulthard, Subjects of Empire? (PhD, 2009), Red Skin, White Masks (2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), 'Land as pedagogy' (2014), As We Have Always Done (2017)

strands.title: Peoplehood against mixedness
strands.focus: Andersen argues that Métis are misrecognised 'as a hybrid off-shoot of two races … rather than as an Indigenous people'. To the question 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?' he answers that 'the racialization of the Métis has never begun nor ended with us'. Peoplehood rests on 'a "national core" historically located in Red River', and 'History is thus a crucial resource in Indigenous claims to peoplehood' (2014). His 2009 essay asks Indigenous studies to start from 'density' rather than 'difference', using disciplines including history. He draws on the historian Brenda Macdougall.
strands.works: Chris Andersen, 'Critical Indigenous Studies: From Difference to Density' (2009); 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (2014)

darcy_mcnickle.label: D’Arcy McNickle
darcy_mcnickle.date_label: NCAI 1944 · They Came Here First 1949 · Workshops from 1960 · Newberry centre 1972 · Native American Tribalism 1973
darcy_mcnickle.description: A writer, administrator and historian, an enrolled member at Flathead (Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes), per Iverson 1993. He helped found the National Congress of American Indians (1944), organised the Workshops on American Indian Affairs from 1960, and chaired the steering committee of the 1961 Chicago conference. They Came Here First (1949) and Native American Tribalism (1973) argued against 'the certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress': Congress in the 1950s had judged that 'Indians had no future as Indians', and termination tried 'to legislate Indians out of existence'. In 1972 he helped create the Newberry Library's centre for Indian history and directed it in its first fellowship year (1973–74). Iverson (1993) noted that 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience'. Vine Deloria Jr. criticised the workshops' approach in 1965.

settler_colonialism.label: Settler colonialism
settler_colonialism.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999, 2006 · journal 2011 · Tuck and Yang 2012 · critiques 2013–14 · TRC 2015 · Wolfe d. 2016 · Englert 2020 · reviewed through 2024
settler_colonialism.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, took land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe gave the field its programme: settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'invasion is a structure not an event' (1999, 2006). Lorenzo Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011) and distinguished colonialism ('you, work for me') from settler colonialism ('you, go away'), adding that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': it 'extinguishes itself'. Two questions organise this selection: how elimination persists while pursuing its own completion, and how settler-colonial analysis relates to Indigenous sovereignty, refusal and resurgence. Veracini develops Wolfe's formula: self-supersession means the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, not a successful decolonisation. The Indigenous reading adopts Wolfe's formula while insisting that 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies' (Kauanui), that 'decolonization is not a metaphor' (Tuck and Yang) and that refusal, not recognition, answers the settler state (Simpson, Coulthard). Settler scholars warn against 'colonial fatalism' (Macoun and Strakosch); Marxists ask whether elimination or exploitation defines the form (Englert). In Canada the frame met an older historiography of reserves, treaties, gender and the state, and the TRC's finding of 'cultural genocide' (2015).
settler_colonialism.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Sayegh (1965), Rodinson (1973), Denoon, Settler Capitalism (1983); Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies (1995). Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999), “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006), “Structure and Event” (2008), Traces of History (2016); Veracini, Settler Colonialism: A Theoretical Overview (2010), “Introducing settler colonial studies” (2011), “Career of a Concept” (2013), The Settler Colonial Present (2015); Elkins and Pedersen, eds. (2005); Cavanagh and Veracini, eds. (2016). Indigenous critique and theory: Byrd (2011), L. B. Simpson (2011, 2017), Tuck and Yang (2012), Coulthard (2014), A. Simpson (2014, 2017), Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014), Moreton-Robinson (2015), Kauanui (2016), Goeman (2016). Critiques: Macoun and Strakosch (2013), Rowse (2014), Greer (2019), Shoemaker (2019), Konishi (2019), Englert (2020), Garba and Sorentino (2020). Canada: Carter (1990, 2008, 2016), Harris (2002, 2004, 2020), Perry (2001, 2015), Miller (2009), Mawani (2009), Regan (2010), Daschuk (2013), McCallum (2014), Battell Lowman and Barker (2015), TRC Summary (2015), Hugill (2017), Burrill (2019), Stanger-Ross, ed. (2020). Jean M. O’Brien, Firsting and Lasting (2010).
settler_colonialism.scope_note: A research field whose consolidation came after 2000; reviewed through 2024 in the period-4 wave (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md). Read in full: Wolfe 2006 (in an Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page), Veracini 2011 and his 2016 obituary of Wolfe, Kauanui 2016, Englert 2020, Goeman 2016; in most pages, Tuck and Yang 2012 and Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014; Macoun and Strakosch 2013 in the authors' version; Veracini 2013 in its author manuscript (abstract, opening, conclusion); the TRC summary pp. 1–3. Unread, known through publisher pages or named readers: Wolfe 1999 beyond pp. 1–2, 2001, 2008, 2016; Veracini 2010, 2015; Coulthard; A. Simpson (book; 2017 abstract read); Byrd; Moreton-Robinson; L. B. Simpson; Rowse; Konishi; Sexton; Garba and Sorentino; King; Daschuk; Miller 2009; Perry 2015; Carter 2016; McCallum; Mawani; Stanger-Ross; Lowman and Barker; Regan. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies; Veracini (2013) and Kauanui (2016) both record uses of the term before Wolfe (Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973, Denoon 1983, Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis 1995). Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris, Miller, Daschuk and McCallum wrote earlier or beside it, and their publisher descriptions do not use the phrase. Critics appear as critics; Kauanui and Goeman defend Wolfe's theory against shallow citation while asking the field to attend to Indigenous studies. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: two or more of the field's authors are cited by 3.2% of Canada + US theses in 2000–09 and 11.0% in 2020–25 (Canada 15.2%, US 6.8%); Wolfe and Veracini are co-cited by 3.0% of theses in 2020–25 and Wolfe with Tuck and Yang, Simpson or Coulthard by 2.3% (the release's category 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' names a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position: Tuck and Yang build on Wolfe, and Kauanui criticises his reception), the only rising two-sided citing after 2000; the Canadian neighbourhood of the founders is the largest and youngest of any field (51 works, median year 2006), its 2020–25 entrants Coulthard, Simpson, Carter, Miller, Daschuk, Kauanui and Greer. strands.title: Structure, not event: the logic of elimination
strands.focus: Wolfe's programme, now read in his own pages. Settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it 'is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'the primary motive for elimination is not race … but access to territory. Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event'; elimination has a 'positive' aspect (allotment, citizenship, child abduction, assimilation) that persists after the frontier, so that the form is 'relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' names its convergence with genocide without 'hierarchy among victims' (2006). The formula goes back to the 1999 book (p. 2) and the 1994 essay (p. 96, per his note 7). Kauanui: the phrase 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement of his theory'.

strands.title: Veracini: the field, the journal and the self-superseding structure
strands.focus: Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011; open access, volunteer-run, on an ARC grant; to Taylor & Francis in 2013) 'to contribute to the consolidation of a new scholarly field'. Colonialism says 'you, work for me'; settler colonialism says 'you, go away'; the two 'should be understood in their dialectical relation'. Developing Wolfe's formula rather than disputing it, he adds that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': 'settler colonialism, by contrast, extinguishes itself' and is 'least visible in the settler cities'. This self-supersession is the settler project's attempted extinction of the settler–Indigenous relation by the disappearance of Indigenous peoples, not a successful decolonisation, which would instead end 'with an indigenous ultimate permanence'; 'decolonisation is not settler decolonisation', and the politics of recognition 'cannot be considered a genuinely decolonising move' (2011). His history of the concept (2013) finds three earlier careers of the term and a consolidation 'from approximately the mid 1990s', with 'both the Canadian and US historiographies … late in adopting' it. Englert calls him Wolfe's 'self-styled intellectual successor'; Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel find in his history 'Indigenous studies and Indigenous resistance … pretty much erased'.

strands.focus: Indigenous political theory read alongside Wolfe in Canadian and US theses, each work with its own target: Tuck and Yang take up Wolfe's formula directly; Coulthard's target is the politics of recognition, Audra Simpson's salvage anthropology and statist recognition, Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's the academy and state education. Tuck and Yang: settler colonialism's violence 'is not temporally contained in the arrival of the settler but is reasserted each day of occupation. This is why Patrick Wolfe (1999) emphasizes that settler colonialism is a structure and not an event'; 'decolonization brings about the repatriation of Indigenous land and life; it is not a metaphor'; the settler–native–slave triad; 'settler moves to innocence'; 'an ethic of incommensurability' against reconciliation, which 'is about rescuing settler normalcy' (2012). Audra Simpson: 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm' and refusal as method (2007, read in full); 'refusal' as 'an alternative to recognition politics in settler colonial society', consent 'as a technique of recognition and simultaneous dispossession' (2017, abstract; the 2014 book is known through Nicoll's review). strands.focus: Kauanui: Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did', yet 'he tends to be most frequently cited as if he had'; 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; indigeneity is 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'; Warrior counted ASA panels and feared the field had become 'an answer to the chronic need for more attention to … Native and Indigenous studies' (2016). Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel: the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study' (2014). Goeman answers from the same field: Wolfe 'critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner' and his work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies' (2016). Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge the field (2019, abstract).

Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).; Corey Snelgrove, Rita Kaur Dhamoon and Jeff Corntassel, "Unsettling Settler Colonialism: The Discourse and Politics of Settlers, and Solidarity with Indigenous Nations," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3, no. 2 (2014): 1–32.

strands.title: Slavery and Black studies critiques
strands.focus: How settler-colonial and decolonial frameworks place slavery and Black people. Wolfe 2006 (read) sets out the opposed racialisations of Black and Indigenous people in the United States; Tuck and Yang's settler–native–slave triad (read) is what Garba and Sorentino answer. Both authors' words are now read; the critics' remain at abstract level.

Wayne Yang's 'Decolonization Is Not a Metaphor'," Antipode 52, no. 3 (2020): 764–782.; Jared Sexton, "The Vel of Slavery: Tracking the Figure of the Unsovereign," Critical Sociology 42, nos. 4–5 (2016): 583–597.; Tiffany Lethabo King, The Black Shoals: Offshore Formations of Black and Native Studies (Durham: Duke University Press, 2019).

strands.title: Structure and its end: Wolfe and Veracini read together
strands.focus: Two emphases within one formula, not a documented exchange between opponents. Wolfe's structure is 'a continuity through time' that 'does not stop' with frontier homicide and 'has not been subject to election results' (2006). Veracini accepts the 'frequently quoted passage' and adds that 'the structure persistently pursues a specific end point' and 'extinguishes itself', so that settler colonialism 'covers its tracks' (2011): the end point is the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, which Veracini distinguishes from decolonisation. The History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) records the two authors co-cited by 3.0% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, a readership pairing that does not itself establish a dispute. Englert reads both as drawing 'a sharp analytical separation' between eliminatory settler and exploitative franchise colonies and finds the separation does not fit Africa or South America (2020); Macoun and Strakosch find in the structure a 'colonial fatalism' and recall the label 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world' (2013): these readings establish different emphases placed on the same structure. Veracini's obituary records Wolfe as 'still a Marxist' of 'the young Marx' for whom 'things are not things in themselves but relationships' (2016).
strands.works: Wolfe, "Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native" (2006); Veracini, "Introducing settler colonial studies" (2011) and "Patrick Wolfe (1949–2016)" (2016); Macoun and Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory" (2013); Englert, "Settlers, Workers, and the Logic of Accumulation by Dispossession" (2020).

strands.title: Canadian history beside and under the frame, 2009–2020
strands.focus: Works that Canadian PhDs read with Wolfe and Veracini, few of which adopt his vocabulary. Treaty history (Miller 2009, a distinctive riser among Canadian PhDs inside the Indigenous family in the 2026-10-23 release), racialisation and law in British Columbia's 'contact zone' (Mawani 2009), settler self-examination after residential schools (Regan 2010; Battell Lowman and Barker 2015: 'Canada and Settler Colonialism', 'It's Always All About the Land'), starvation policy (Daschuk 2013), Indigenous women's work 'in modern Native ways' (McCallum 2014), the TRC's finding that Canada's policy aimed 'to eliminate Aboriginal governments … and … cause Aboriginal peoples to cease to exist as distinct … entities' and 'can best be described as "cultural genocide"' (2015), imperial family and archive (Perry 2015), women homesteaders in 'the spadework of British colonialism' who 'took part in dispossessing Indigenous people' (Carter 2016), the settler-colonial city (Hugill 2017), the settler order in working-class history (Burrill 2019), Japanese Canadian dispossession (Stanger-Ross 2020), and Harris's reflections (2020). Veracini's own history says the Canadian historiography was 'late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis' (2013). Publisher descriptions, not the books, are read; none of Miller, Daschuk, McCallum, Perry 2015, Carter 2016 or Stanger-Ross uses the phrase on its page.

strands.title: A field's institutions: journal, associations, memorials
strands.focus: NAISA founded 2008 after an ASA panel of 2002 asked whether American Studies could be 'an intellectual home' for Native studies (Kauanui). Settler Colonial Studies founded 2011 'in an open access format (entirely run on volunteer labour)' and moved to Taylor & Francis 'within two years' (Snelgrove et al.; Edmonds and Carey 2013). Wolfe edited paired issues of the journal and of AICRJ (2013) and answered the binary charge with The Settler Complex (2016). ASA 2015: Goldstein's reappraisal and Warrior's count of panels. Wolfe's death (18 February 2016) brought obituaries from the journal (Veracini), AICRJ (Goeman), Aboriginal History (Birch) and an American Quarterly forum (2017); a Festschrift followed (Race, Place, Trace, 2022).

glen_coulthard.label: Glen Sean Coulthard
glen_coulthard.date_label: Subjects of Empire? (PhD) 2009 · Red Skin, White Masks 2014
glen_coulthard.description: A Yellowknives Dene political theorist whose critique of recognition is read by historians of colonial Canada. His 2009 dissertation, the basis of Red Skin, White Masks (2014), set out 'to challenge the now commonplace assumption that the colonial relationship between Indigenous peoples and Canada can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition', using Fanon's critique of Hegel against the liberal recognition that Charles Taylor defended. Reworking Marx's primitive accumulation, he argued that 'the history and experience of dispossession, not proletarianization' had shaped relations with the Canadian state, and that Indigenous anti-colonialism is 'a struggle primarily inspired by and oriented around the question of land'. His alternative, self-recognition, means 'critically revaluating, reconstructing and redeploying Indigenous cultural forms'. He named Taiaiake Alfred, with James Tully, as a mentor.

emma_larocque.label: Emma LaRocque
emma_larocque.date_label: Defeathering the Indian 1975 · dissertation 1999 · When the Other Is Me 2011
emma_larocque.description: A Plains Cree Métis scholar whose criticism of Canadian historical writing began with school textbooks. Her 1974 research for Alberta found 'endless layers of stereotypes … particularly in history and social studies' and led to Defeathering the Indian (1975). Her 1999 dissertation named its targets. James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing was 'eye-opening and ground-breaking' but 'does not go deep enough', for 'Canadian historiography is not that benign'. Trigger's foreword to Sioui's Autohistory showed 'a language of containment'. The 'neo cross-cultural approach' of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk framed 'all things Native' as 'cultural differences'. Scholars, 'especially historians and literary critics', must 'comprehend the noxious nature of colonization before dismissing utterances of decolonization'. She drew on Memmi, Fanon and Said, and on Howard Adams's 'White Ideal'. When the Other Is Me (2011) is the revised book.

chris_andersen.label: Chris Andersen
chris_andersen.description: A Michif (Métis) sociologist whose 'Métis' (2014) challenges the understanding of Métis as 'mixed'. Scholars of 'Métis histories, literatures, and politics' are drawn to 'simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity'; to the question 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?' he answers that 'the racialization of the Métis has never begun nor ended with us', but belonged to colonial projects to 'usurp all the Indigenous territories' on which Canada was built. Peoplehood rests instead on 'a "national core" historically located in Red River', and 'History is thus a crucial resource in Indigenous claims to peoplehood'. He draws on the historian Brenda Macdougall. His 2009 essay asked Indigenous studies to start from 'density' rather than 'difference', using the disciplines, history among them, that communities themselves use.

winona_wheeler.label: Winona Wheeler
winona_wheeler.date_label: 'The Othering of Indigenous History' 1998 · 'Reflections on the Social Relations of Indigenous Oral History' 2005 · 'Cree Intellectual Traditions in History' 2010 · Shekon Neechie 2018 · open letter 2021
winona_wheeler.description: Cree historian (Fisher River Cree Nation) of oral tradition and of the academy's treatment of Indigenous history. In 1998 she argued that historians of 'Indian–White relations', relying on the records of one side, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist frame. Her method writing treats Indigenous oral history 'as source and method in scholarly research': elders 'are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers', and the historian 'develops reciprocal relationships with them'. Oral historians, she argues, must learn how knowledge keepers establish their sources ('a traditional footnote'), and the historian's task is 'to apply the teachings that guide the learning, keeping, and transmission of Indigenous knowledge' (2010). She learned from Stan Cuthand, Ahenakew's protégé, and draws on Ahenakew's published account of Old Men as historians. Leddy (2010) opens her account of community-based history with Wheeler's words on knowledge 'by way of relationships'. She serves on the managing board of Shekon Neechie (2018).

brenda_macdougall.label: Brenda Macdougall
brenda_macdougall.date_label: One of the Family 2010 · Clio Prize 2011 · 'Ways of Knowing' symposium 2018 · open letter 2021
brenda_macdougall.description: Métis historian of family and community in the northwest. One of the Family (2010) set out 'to contribute … to the development of methodologies and models by which we could interpret historical documents in a manner that reflected the perspectives, realities, and experiences of Aboriginal communities'. She read fur-trade, mission and scrip records through wahkootowin, a concept she credits to Métis Elder Maria Campbell and frames as a Cree worldview of 'relatedness' that 'did not appear in any of the historical records'. Against a historiography 'overly preoccupied with race at the expense of culture', she showed Métis people 'actively involved in becoming, rather than passively awaiting identity transmission through external forces and trauma'. In 2018 she co-hosted a symposium on Métis-specific research methods.

robert_alexander_innes.label: Robert Alexander Innes
robert_alexander_innes.date_label: Oral history methods 1999–2000 · insider/outsider 2009 · Elder Brother and the Law of the People 2013 · 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' and 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' 2018 · open letter 2021
robert_alexander_innes.description: Cowessess First Nation historian of kinship and treaty land, and a critic of how historians have written the 1880s starvation policy. In 2018 he wrote that neither historians nor the Canadian government had acknowledged the starvation deaths of the early 1880s in Treaty 4 territory as genocide, and that historians who agreed the policy killed many had not tried to count the dead. Cowessess First Nation's own treaty land entitlement research had done that work. Historical records, he argued, do not tell a story by themselves, and decolonizing history can simply mean asking the right questions and looking in the right places. Against Daschuk's Clearing the Plains (2013), he held that Edgar Dewdney bore responsibility and that Daschuk misrepresented Tobias, Lux and Titley, whom he cites. Earlier he wrote on oral history methods in Native Studies and on insider research; he conceived Shekon Neechie (2018).
robert_alexander_innes.representative_figures_and_works: Robert Alexander Innes; 'Oral History Methods in Native Studies' (Oral History Forum, 1999–2000); 'Wait a Second. Who Are You Anyways?' mary_jane_logan_mccallum.label: Mary Jane Logan McCallum
mary_jane_logan_mccallum.date_label: 'Indigenous Labor and Indigenous History' 2009 · Indigenous Women, Work, and History 2014 · 'Words for Reading Indigenous Health History' 2017 · 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' 2018 · open letter 2021
mary_jane_logan_mccallum.description: Munsee Delaware historian of Indigenous labour, health and archives. Indigenous Women, Work, and History (2014) follows domestic workers, hairdressers, community health representatives and nurses through state placement programmes, 1940–80; her reviewer Carol Williams notes that she worked with nursing associations who 'granted full access to records', and that her conclusion 'reflects on the professional status and glaring absence of Indigenous historians in academia'. Writing in 2018, she treats archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians: Indian Affairs records were made without Indigenous knowledge or consent, yet remain vital to Indigenous history. She describes interpreting such records together with others rather than alone, and hopes for Indigenous roles in making and keeping records. She sits on the managing board of Shekon Neechie.

life_lived_like_a_story.label: Life Lived Like a Story (Sidney, Smith, Ned and Cruikshank, 1990)
life_lived_like_a_story.date_label: Family request 1974 · UBC Press and Nebraska 1990 · paperback 1992 · reviewed 1992 · cited as a model 2009–10
life_lived_like_a_story.description: A book credited to Julie Cruikshank 'in collaboration with' three Yukon elders, Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned, who told their life stories; Cruikshank recorded and arranged them. The project began in 1974, when 'younger members of their respective families … asked Cruikshank to record their autobiographies' (McClellan 1992). The narrators chose the form: Sidney and Smith wove personal incidents with 'well-known stories from the traditional narrative repertoire', and Ned 'chose to emphasize songs and oratory'. Cruikshank, Gmelch wrote, 'gradually shifted her research focus from documenting their lives … to examining the actual way they talked about, remembered, and interpreted their lives'. Reviewers called it 'a work of true collaboration between native and non-native' and 'a valuable model of how collaboration between an anthropologist or oral historian and their native teachers can work'; McClellan also noted that Cruikshank 'selected the material' and 'arranged it'.
life_lived_like_a_story.representative_figures_and_works: Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith, Annie Ned and Julie Cruikshank, Life Lived Like a Story: Life Stories of Three Yukon Native Elders (Vancouver: UBC Press; Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 1990; Bison paperback 1992). Readers: Catharine McClellan (Arctic, 1992); Sharon Gmelch (BC Studies, 1992); Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe (2009); Leddy (2010).
life_lived_like_a_story.scope_note: A packaged collaborative entry (user decision, 2026-10-27): the four are credited together as the book credits them ('in collaboration with'), not as a Cruikshank person entry. The entry rests on the publisher description and two contemporary reviews read in full (McClellan, Arctic 45:2, 1992, 205–206; Gmelch, BC Studies 94, 1992, 85–86); Cruikshank's words are given only 'as quoted by' them.
